summary.text:
The largest balance sheet we have read so far, and the one with the least prose around it. Barnsley's treasury position reaches the public as a single appendix of tables — no narrative, no commentary, no explanation. The figures are complete and they reconcile; what is missing is anyone saying what they mean.

At 30 September 2025 the capital financing requirement was £1,088.9m — £562.7m General Fund, £271.7m HRA, and £254.5m of other long-term liabilities, which is PFI and leases rather than borrowing. Gross external debt was £561.9m. Setting the PFI aside, that leaves roughly £272m funded internally.

The number that should stop a reader is the HRA. Financing costs take 37.80% of the HRA's net revenue stream — more than a third of the rent roll before a single repair is done. The General Fund ratio is 15.37%, though 7.28% of that is PFI: strip the PFI out and the General Fund runs at 7.28%, which is unremarkable. The HRA figure has no such qualifier, and the HRA's CFR did not move at all over the period — annual change of exactly zero.

The debt is very long and therefore very cheap to hold. 89% of the General Fund book runs beyond ten years, with 44% at 40–50 years and 25% at 30–40; the HRA is 89% beyond ten years with 54% at 30–40. Only 2% of either falls due within a year. This is historic PWLB, locked in, and it is why a council with £562m of debt is not in the news. The corollary is that almost none of it can be refinanced at today's rates even if a treasurer wanted to.

Two things sit oddly. The authorised limit is set at £1,122.3m against actual external debt of £730.6m — headroom of nearly £400m, on a limit that is supposed to be a control. And the capital programme had delivered £39.6m of a £154.3m plan at the half year: 26%, with the second half expected to carry the other 74%.

One practical warning for anyone reading the paper itself. Its indicator tables are headed £'000 and the figures are in fact £m — the maturity tables immediately below are correctly labelled (£M) and total to the same number. Read literally, the header understates everything by a factor of a thousand.

officer.subject: Your Cabinet on 9 September — three questions members may put to you on the indicators
officer.body:
Dear Colleague,

Your Cabinet meets on Wednesday 9 September. We read council treasury papers and track PWLB rates every working day, and we have been through Barnsley's treasury and prudential indicators.

A note on what we could and could not read, because it shapes everything below. The most recent indicators we can find are Q2 2025/26, taken to Cabinet in December. They are complete and they reconcile — gross external debt of £561.914m against General Fund and HRA maturity tables totalling £561.915m, and a CFR of £1,088.905m that sums exactly from its three components. What they carry is figures alone: no commentary, no explanation of what moved, and nothing on what the numbers mean for the year ahead.

Three questions we would expect from a member who has worked through them.

1. The HRA financing ratio. Financing costs take 37.80% of the HRA's net revenue stream. The General Fund figure is 15.37%, and the paper helpfully separates the PFI element to show 7.28% underneath it. The HRA figure carries no such qualifier, the HRA CFR did not move at all over the period — an annual change of exactly zero — and 89% of the HRA book runs beyond ten years, 54% of it at 30 to 40 years. So the ratio cannot be brought down by refinancing. The question is what the thirty-year business plan assumes and at what level it stops being affordable.

2. The authorised limit. It is set at £1,122.285m against actual external debt of £730.577m — headroom of nearly £400m on the one borrowing control full Council sets for itself. Set far enough above the position, a limit stops being a decision. Worth being able to say what it is controlling for and what would have to happen to approach it.

3. Capital delivery. £39.557m of a £154.320m programme was spent at the half year — 26%, with 74% expected in the second half. Members reading the same table will ask what was actually delivered by 31 March and how much slipped, because that determines both the CFR and the MRP charge, and the published indicators stop at Q2.

Two practical points, offered as help rather than criticism. The indicator tables are headed £'000 while the figures are £m — the maturity tables immediately below are correctly labelled (£M) and total to the same number, which is how we spotted it. Read literally, the header understates the council by a factor of a thousand, and it is in the version members have. And every other council we have read this year publishes a short narrative alongside its indicators. A member cannot challenge a 37.80% HRA financing ratio that arrives as one unlabelled cell.

On what borrowing costs now, for context: the PWLB 10-year maturity rate struck at 6.02% this morning, notice 309/26, with 25-year at 6.65%. Barnsley's book is long and historic, so almost none of it is exposed to that — which is the strongest thing in this position and worth saying out loud.

Every figure above is from Barnsley's own appendix or from today's PWLB fixing, and we will send page references for any of them.

A word on who we are, since this arrived unasked. PWLBtoday tracks PWLB rates every working day and reads the treasury papers of every council that publishes them. We do not sell treasury products and we do not advise on borrowing. There is a training library alongside it, for officers and for members. The courses your papers point to are listed with this email, each with the figure that put it there.

With best wishes,

PWLBtoday
pwlbtoday.org

member.subject: Your Cabinet meets 9 September — a third of the rent roll goes on debt
member.body:
Dear Councillor,

Your Cabinet meets on Wednesday 9 September. We read council treasury papers and track PWLB borrowing rates every working day, and we have read Barnsley's.

First, the good news, because it is the larger part of the story. Barnsley's debt is old, long and cheap. **89% of it runs beyond ten years** — 44% of the General Fund book does not mature for 40 to 50 years — and only 2% falls due within a year. Councils borrowing today pay around 6%; Barnsley locked in its borrowing when money was far cheaper. That is why a council with £561.9m of debt is not in the newspapers, and whoever arranged it did the authority a real service.

The figure that should stop you is on the housing side. **Financing costs take 37.80% of the Housing Revenue Account's net revenue stream.** More than a third of the rent your tenants pay goes on servicing debt before a single repair is done.

For comparison, the General Fund figure is 15.37%, and the report is careful to show that most of that is PFI — strip it out and the General Fund runs at 7.28%. The HRA figure comes with no such explanation. **What does the thirty-year housing business plan assume for that ratio, and at what level does the council consider it unaffordable?**

This matters more than it would elsewhere, because it cannot be fixed by refinancing. The HRA's debt is 89% long-dated too, so there is no cheaper deal to move to and no early exit that would not cost a penalty. The ratio is what it is until the debt is repaid.

Two others worth asking.

**What is the borrowing limit actually limiting?** Full Council sets an authorised limit — the legal ceiling on what the authority may owe. Barnsley's is £1,122.3m. Its actual debt is £730.6m. That is close to £400m of headroom on the one borrowing control councillors set themselves.

**Where did the capital programme end up?** At the half-year point £39.6m of a £154.3m programme had been spent — 26%, with the other 74% due in the remaining six months. Either it accelerated sharply or a lot of it slipped into this year. The published figures stop at that halfway point, so the answer is not in front of you.

One last thing, and it is a fair request rather than a complaint. These figures reach you as an appendix of tables with no words around them — no explanation of what changed or why. The tables are also headed £'000 when the figures are actually £m, which we only caught because a table further down is labelled correctly and totals to the same number. **Could future reports include a short commentary, and correct the heading?** Most councils we read do.

Every figure above comes from Barnsley's own published appendix, and we are happy to send page references for all of them.

A word on who we are, since this arrived unasked. PWLBtoday tracks PWLB rates every working day and reads the treasury papers of every council that publishes them. We do not sell treasury products, we do not advise councils on borrowing, and we have no view on what Barnsley should do — which is why we can put the numbers and the questions in front of you and leave the judgement to you. There is also a training library, including short courses written for members rather than accountants.

If any of this is useful, or if you want the page references, just reply.

With best wishes,

PWLBtoday
pwlbtoday.org
